Definition_of_value_1: The sound-producing vibration comes from one or more stretched strings.
The sound-producing vibration is that of air itself, either an enclosed air column or a free reed.
The sound-producing vibration is that of a stretched membrane.
The body of the instrument itself vibrates to produce the sound.
The strings are normally set in motion with a bow.
The strings are normally set in motion by plucking or strumming, by fingers, plectrum or an internal quill mechanism.
The strings are normally set in motion by hammers or beaters.
Sound is excited by one or more beating single reeds under the player's control.
Sound is excited by a double reed.
Sound is produced by free reeds vibrating in a frame, with no associated air column.
Sound is excited by the player's buzzing lips.
Sound is excited by an air stream directed against a sharp edge or through a fipple, with no reed and no lip buzzing.
The player supplies air directly with the mouth, into or across the instrument or a blowpipe.
Air is supplied by bellows, a blower or an air-reservoir bag rather than by the mouth alone.
Normally sounded by striking with sticks, mallets or beaters.
Normally sounded by striking with the bare hands or fingers.
Normally sounded by shaking, or by clashing two parts of the instrument together.
The fingerboard carries frets or comparable fixed stopping points.
Pitch is changed with piston or rotary valves.
Pitch is changed with a movable slide.
The instrument has tone holes closed by the fingers directly or by keys.
The instrument is played from a piano-style keyboard of keys.
One or more foot pedals are part of normal playing technique.
Produces a clearly recognisable musical pitch rather than an indefinite-pitched sound.
All twelve semitones are available throughout the instrument's normal range in ordinary playing.
A single player can sound at least three different pitches at the same moment.
Pitch can be varied smoothly across a wide span rather than only in fixed steps.
A note can be held at steady volume for as long as the player continues the exciting action.
The instrument cannot produce its normal sound without electrical power.
The sound reaching the listener is generated or transduced electrically rather than radiated acoustically by the instrument itself.
A regular member of the standard symphony orchestra.
A regular member of the standard Western wind band.
Commonly used in jazz ensembles.
Commonly used in rock and popular-music bands.
Music is conventionally written at a pitch other than it sounds, including octave transpositions.
The instrument's design or size normally requires or strongly favours playing while seated.
Commonly played while marching or moving in procession.
The body or main resonating structure is made primarily of wood, bamboo or cane.
The body or main sounding structure is made primarily of metal.
Has a hollow soundbox, shell, soundboard or tuned resonator that amplifies a separately vibrating element (0 for aerophones).
The instrument in its recognised form developed in a tradition outside Europe.
The instrument came into existence after 1900.
